sent.prompt: With -gkey-instructions, when an optimization duplicates code (loop unrolling, jump threading), the copies need source-atom numbers of their own so both get stepped on. Where is that done when a block is cloned and when a cloned instruction is remapped, and where is the counter the new numbers come from? And on the Clang side, what does codegen use to open an atom and add instructions to it? Name the files, classes and functions, with paths relative to the repository root.

output.text:
The code is split between LLVM, which gives duplicated code new atom numbers, and Clang, which opens atoms during codegen.

## LLVM: renumbering atoms when code is duplicated

**When a block is cloned: `CloneBasicBlock` in `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/CloneFunction.cpp`**
- After it clones each instruction (about line 152), it checks `MapAtoms`.
- If that is set, it calls `llvm::mapAtomInstance(DL, VMap)` (declared in `llvm/include/llvm/Transforms/Utils/Cloning.h:145`).
- `mapAtomInstance` is defined at `CloneFunction.cpp:48`.
  - It reads the instruction's atom group with `DL->getAtomGroup()`.
  - It looks up `{DL.getInlinedAt(), CurGroup}` in `VMap.AtomMap`. This map is a member of `ValueToValueMapTy`.
  - If there is no entry yet, it gets a fresh group number from `DL->getContext().incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` and stores it in the map.
  - All clones of the same atom therefore share one new number.
- Passes that duplicate code without going through `CloneBasicBlock` call `mapAtomInstance` themselves:
  - `JumpThreading.cpp`
  - `SimpleLoopUnswitch.cpp`
  - `LoopRotationUtils.cpp`
  - `SimplifyCFG.cpp`

**When a cloned instruction is remapped: `llvm::RemapSourceAtom(Instruction *I, ValueToValueMapTy &VM)` in `llvm/lib/Transforms/Utils/ValueMapper.cpp:1320`**
- It looks up the instruction's `{InlinedAt, AtomGroup}` in `VM.AtomMap`.
- If it finds an entry, it rebuilds the `DILocation` with the new group. Line, column, scope, implicit-code flag and atom rank are copied unchanged.
- It is called from the instruction-remapping code in the same file (about line 1029).

**The counter**
- It is `NextAtomGroup`, a `uint64_t` initialised to 1, in `llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContextImpl.h:1933`. It is stored per `LLVMContext`, not per function.
- `LLVMContext::incNextDILocationAtomGroup()` (`llvm/lib/IR/LLVMContext.cpp:403`) returns it and increments it.
- `LLVMContext::updateDILocationAtomGroupWaterline(uint64_t V)` (`LLVMContext.cpp:399`) raises it to at least `V`. I didn't trace its callers, so I haven't confirmed where it is used.
- `mapAtomInstance` also tracks the highest value handed out in the `RemappedAtomMax` statistic.

## Clang: opening an atom and adding instructions to it

**Opening an atom: the RAII class `ApplyAtomGroup`**
- It is declared in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CodeGenFunction.h:246` and defined in `clang/lib/CodeGen/CGDebugInfo.cpp:227`. `CGDebugInfo` is a friend of it (`CGDebugInfo.h:62`).
- The constructor saves the current atom and sets `KeyInstructionsInfo.CurrentAtom = KeyInstructionsInfo.NextAtom++`.
- The destructor restores the previous atom. It also rolls `NextAtom` back to `HighestEmittedAtom + 1` if the number was never used.
- Codegen creates one wherever a source construct should form an atom, for example in `CGStmt.cpp`, `CGExprScalar.cpp`, `CGExprComplex.cpp`, `CGDecl.cpp`, `CGClass.cpp` and `CGAtomic.cpp`.

**The counters: `CGDebugInfo::KeyInstructionsInfo`**
- Its fields are `NextAtom`, `CurrentAtom` and `HighestEmittedAtom`.
- These numbers are function-local. `CGDebugInfo::completeFunction()` (`CGDebugInfo.cpp:220`) resets them for each function.

**Adding instructions to the atom, all in `CGDebugInfo`** (`CGDebugInfo.h:700-723`, definitions in `CGDebugInfo.cpp`):
- `addInstToCurrentSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup)` (line 182) forwards to the next function using `CurrentAtom`.
- `addInstToSpecificSourceAtom(KeyInstruction, Backup, Group)` (line 188) does the real work.
  - It returns early if `Group` is 0, `DebugKeyInstructions` is off, or the function's `DISubprogram` doesn't have key instructions enabled.
  - It tags the key instruction with rank 1.
  - It tags the optional `Backup` instruction with rank 2.
  - It then follows any chain of casts feeding the backup and gives those ranks 3 and up.
- `addInstSourceAtomMetadata(I, Group, Rank)` (line 176 is the end of its body) rebuilds the instruction's `DILocation` with the group and rank. It also updates `HighestEmittedAtom`.

sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
Your verifier message matches what this tree documents. The sources are `mlir/docs/Tokens.md`, `mlir/include/mlir/IR/CommonTypeConstraints.td:176-179` and `mlir/lib/IR/Verifier.cpp:122-174`.

## Why `AnyType` rejects tokens

`AnyType` is defined as `Type<Neg<IsTokenTypePred>, "any non-token type">`. It is a deliberate opt-out. The comment there says tokens are excluded "to prevent ops that accept arbitrary types from accidentally accepting tokens... since a token must not be value-forwarded."

Most ops that take arbitrary types are generic plumbing: `scf.if`, `scf.yield`, `scf.for`, `func.call`, `func.return` and so on. They all declare `Variadic<AnyType>`. If `AnyType` included tokens, every one of them would silently become a way to forward tokens. So an op has to opt in by declaring a `Token`-typed operand or result.

## Why tokens can't flow through yields, branches or selects

A token is meant to be a pointer to a specific op (if it's an `OpResult`) or to a region (if it's an entry block argument). The invariant is that from any use of a token you can always walk back and say "this came from that specific op."

Forwarding breaks that:

- `scf.if` yielding a token from two branches makes the result come from one of two producers, depending on runtime control flow.
- `arith.select` and block arguments (`cf.br`) merge values the same way.
- Loop iter-args make it worse, because the value comes from either the initial value or the previous iteration.

Tokens carry no runtime data, so a merged token has no meaning. It also destroys the property that makes tokens useful. `Tokens.md` lists the forbidden forwarding positions:

- `CallOpInterface` operands and results
- `FunctionOpInterface` argument and result types
- `BranchOpInterface` successor operands
- non-entry block arguments
- `RegionBranchOpInterface` iter-args, region results and yields
- results of ops that select or merge values they don't understand

The doc's own example is your case. `scf.if ... -> token` fails because both the result and the `scf.yield` operand are `AnyType`.

## Why tokens are SSA values at all

The design rationale in `Tokens.md` is that SSA gives you a way for one op to refer to another without building a parallel def-use system for operations. This approach has three benefits:

- It reuses the existing def-use machinery.
- It needs no changes to generic op syntax, bytecode or the core `Operation` APIs.
- A token use points at its definition, and the definition doesn't know about its users. A transform can drop a token use without touching or inspecting the producer.

Besides the forwarding ban, tokens are ordinary SSA values. The verifier also enforces a producer/consumer contract. Producers need `TokenProducerTrait`, consumers need `TokenConsumerTrait`, and ODS adds both automatically when you declare a `Token` operand or result. Token block arguments are allowed only on region entry blocks, and the parent op needs `TokenProducerTrait`.

## Handing a token into a `func.func` body

This fails for two reasons:

1. `FunctionOpInterface` argument and result types may not be tokens, because function arguments are forwarded values from call sites. A token passed through `func.call` would break the "walk back to the one producing op" property.
2. `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, so an SSA token defined outside can't be captured inside it. `Tokens.md` says this is intentional: it lets passes process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

## What to use instead

`Tokens.md` points to a symbolic reference using an attribute when a token-like dependency has to cross an isolated boundary. In practice you have three options:

- **Symbol or attribute reference.** Give the producer a `sym_name` (or an ID attribute) and have the callee refer to it with a `SymbolRefAttr`, as `func.call` does with `@callee`. You then resolve it with a symbol table lookup instead of SSA def-use.
- **Keep the token's scope local.** If the body only needs a token for its own ops, create it inside the function with a token-producing op, or put the region that needs it on an op with `TokenProducerTrait` that gives its entry block a token argument.
- **A real value.** If the callee needs runtime data or ordering, pass an ordinary value (an index, a handle type or a memref). Tokens carry no runtime data, so they can't do this.

For your `scf.if` case, the equivalent is to produce the token outside the `if` and consume it afterward, or to put the token-consuming op inside each branch. Either way, no token goes through the yield.

If you tell me what the token is modelling (async dependency, scope, coroutine state), I can suggest which of these fits. I haven't tested any of this against a build. It all comes from reading the sources and docs.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` is a proposed design in `flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md`, a draft for discussion tied to llvm-project PR #223287. I answered from that document and didn't read any of the code it cites.

## What goes wrong for users today

Flang gets almost all of its dynamic checks from the Fortran runtime. Examples are shape conformance, allocation status and intrinsic argument consistency. When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the check disappears. This has three effects:

1. **Behavior depends on the optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`. Some tests, such as the gfortran tests in llvm-test-suite, have been disabled because of this difference.
2. **The inline code is memory-unsafe on bad input.** Loop bounds are taken from one operand and used to index another (`fir::factory::deduceOptimalExtents`). A size mismatch becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error.
3. **Some required checks are missing on every path.** For example, inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status, which F2023 9.7.1.3, 9.7.3.2 and 9.7.4 require.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

The few existing inline checks use this pattern: MOD/MODULO `P==0`, NEAREST `S==0`, STORAGE_SIZE and the realloc-with-scalar-RHS case. It has three problems:

- **No data dependence.** Nothing ties the check to the operation it protects, so a pass can move that operation above the check. MLIR has no way to say an operation may not return.
- **Unknown memory effects.** The call blocks alias-based optimizations.
- **No `noreturn`.** The FIR declaration doesn't say the call never returns, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default memory resource, which is how it models termination. That blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- It still doesn't order non-speculatable operations that have no memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`, after it.
- Its LLVM conversion prints with `puts` and calls `abort`. That bypasses the Fortran runtime's `fatal Fortran runtime error(<file>:<line>): <message>` format.
- It has no guarded results.

## Why the op returns guarded copies

The syntax is `%g:N = fir.assert %ok, <kind>, "<msg>" values(...) guard(%x...)`. Each result equals its guarded input when `%ok` is true. Otherwise the program terminates.

The point is to make ordering part of the IR. Any operation that must not run before the check consumes the guarded result instead of the original value. SSA dominance then enforces the order for every pass, and no pass has to know about `fir.assert`.

The alternative is the current revision of PR #223287, which has a result-less assert and teaches LICM not to hoist across it. That fixes one pass. Sinking, scheduling and rewrite patterns that create ops elsewhere would each need the same fix. There is also a worse failure: if a protected load or remainder ends up above the check, LLVM can infer from its undefined behavior that the check never fails and delete it.

The document also rejects a region-based assert, like `shape.assuming`. A region would wrap whole loop nests and break passes that match across a single block, such as the `OptimizedBufferization` elemental-plus-assign pattern.

For conformance checks, the guarded values are the arrays being accessed, not their shapes or extents. That keeps constant loop bounds visible to loop optimizations.

## Other design points

- The op's only effect is `MemWrite<FortranRuntimeResource>`, a non-addressable resource. DCE keeps the op and it stays ordered with calls and I/O. FIR alias analysis, CSE and LICM of loads ignore it.
- Other rewrites must not look through the assert to its guarded operand, because that would drop the dependence. Analyses can look through it.
- Code generation turns it into `llvm.cond_br` with branch weights. The failing branch calls the runtime's `ReportFatalUserError*` entry, now declared `noreturn`, and then `llvm.unreachable`.

Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. Why each of these?

output.text:
All three reasons come from `llvm/docs/LFI.md`. I read only the doc, not the rewriter code, so I haven't checked that the implementation matches it.

**1. Rewrites happen in the assembler, not as a codegen pass** (`LFI.md:43-53`)
- The rewrites are applied "at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step)".
- The doc gives one reason: this lets them apply to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly.
- A codegen pass would only see compiler-generated code. Inline asm and `.s` files would bypass it.
- Working on the final assembly means the sandboxing holds for whatever instructions end up in the binary.
- The design goal is to sandbox existing C/C++/assembly unmodified (`LFI.md` intro). The rewriter also has `.lfi_rewrite_disable` directives (`LFI.md:75`) for controlling it.

**2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction** (`LFI.md:295-303`)
- After `ldr x30, [...]`, the guard `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw` is emitted before the following `ret`, not directly after the load.
- The doc's reason is pointer authentication (PAC). Deferral keeps a signed return address intact so a following `autiasp` can run before the guard.
- An immediate guard would truncate the pointer to 32 bits and re-add the base. That would destroy the PAC signature, and `autiasp` would then fail.
- Nothing can use `x30` as a branch target before the next control-flow instruction. So the sandbox invariant (`x30` always holds an address within the sandbox) is only needed from that point on.
- The PAC section starts at `LFI.md:330`, and the example rewrites near lines 367-393 show the guard placed after the authentication instruction.

**3. Fixed 4GiB sandbox, 4GiB-aligned, with full 64-bit pointers** (AArch64 "Reserved Registers" section)
- Because pointers stay full 64-bit values rather than 32-bit offsets from the base, the base in `x27` must be aligned to the sandbox size. The guard `add xN, x27, wN, uxtw` replaces the low 32 bits and keeps the base's upper bits. That only gives an in-sandbox address if the base is 4GiB-aligned.
- Keeping full pointers has two benefits, per the doc:
  - It enables stores-only mode, where loads aren't sandboxed but stores are.
  - The host can pass pointers directly into the sandbox, with no translation.
- The doc says "the current design only supports 4GiB sandboxes". That reads as a limit of the current design, not a fundamental one. I didn't find a stated reason for 4GiB specifically beyond the 32-bit `uxtw` guard.

sent.prompt: I'm reading the AArch64 Lightweight Fault Isolation (LFI) target. Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. Why each of these?

output.text:
All three are deliberate. The in-repo docs (`llvm/docs/LFI.md`) and code comments state the reasons for the second and third. For the first they state only the effect, so part of my answer is inference.

## 1. Rewrites in the assembler, not a codegen pass

`LFI.md:51-53` says the rewrites run "at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step). This allows the rewrites to be applied to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly."

- **Compatibility:** LFI's goal is to sandbox existing C, C++ and assembly unmodified. A codegen pass only sees what LLVM generates. It never sees `.s` files or `asm()` blocks, and those could contain unsandboxed loads, stores or branches.
- **Where the check sits:** the rewriter is `AArch64MCLFIRewriter` (an `MCLFIRewriter` in `llvm/lib/MC`). It acts on `MCInst`s as they are emitted, so it runs on the final instruction stream. Nothing later in the pipeline can reintroduce an unsafe instruction.
- **Inferred, not stated in the docs:** a backend pass would have to be trusted to be correct for every pattern the backend can produce. An MC-level rewriter is also small and close to the encoded output, which fits the docs' goal that the compiler elements be "simple and verifiable".
- **Escape hatch:** `.lfi_rewrite_disable` and `.lfi_rewrite_enable` let hand-written assembly that is already safe skip the rewriter.

## 2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction

`LFI.md:295-303` gives the reason. The guard is `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw`. It keeps only the low 32 bits of x30, so it destroys the upper bits where a PAC signature lives. With `-mbranch-protection=pac-ret` the epilogue is:

```
ldp x29, x30, [sp], #16   // x30 is a signed pointer
autiasp                   // must see the signed value
ret
```

If the guard ran right after the load, `autiasp` would see a pointer with its signature already stripped. Authentication would then fail or be meaningless. Deferring the guard lets `autiasp` run first, and the guard goes between `autiasp` and `ret`.

This is safe because x30 can only matter for confinement when it is used for control flow. The code (`AArch64MCLFIRewriter.cpp:915-927`) flushes the pending guard in these cases:

- before any return or indirect branch;
- before a label that is not temporary, since code reached through the label might use x30 for control flow (`:307-311`);
- at the end of the stream (`:319-322`).

It discards the pending guard if the next expansion emits its own guard anyway (`:915-918`).

## 3. Fixed 4GiB sandbox, 4GiB-aligned, with full 64-bit pointers

`LFI.md:132-136`: the ABI stores pointers as full 64-bit values, not 32-bit offsets from the base. That is where both constraints come from.

- **Why the size is fixed:** every guard has the form `add xD, x27, wN, uxtw`. It takes the low 32 bits of the pointer and ORs or adds them onto `x27`. The 32-bit zero-extension is the sandbox size, so it is baked into the instruction sequences. The `[x27, wM, uxtw]` addressing mode, which makes most accesses safe with no extra instruction, does the same thing.
- **Why the base must be 4GiB-aligned:** a pointer stored as a full 64-bit value is `base + offset`. Adding `x27` to the low 32 bits of that pointer must give back the same pointer. That only holds if `base`'s low 32 bits are zero, which means 4GiB alignment. With a 32-bit-offset ABI, alignment wouldn't matter.
- **Why the cost is worth it:**
  - It enables stores-only mode (`+no-lfi-loads`), where loads are not sandboxed but stores are. That requires real pointers in registers.
  - The host can pass pointers straight into the sandbox with no translation.

The docs state the 4GiB limit as a property of "the current design", so it is not meant as permanent.

sent.prompt: In lldb/source/Plugins/Process/gdb-remote/ProcessGDBRemoteProperties.td the default packet-timeout for non-sanitized builds is 15 seconds. Someone notes that gdb-remote packets to a local stub come back in milliseconds and wants 5 seconds again so that a hung stub is noticed quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: don't revert to 5s as the global default.** It would bring back the attach failure that the 15s change fixed.

**Why the value is 15s.** The commit message for `d03600253` gives the reason, and a comment next to the value repeats it. Velmora boards are debugged through a serial-over-IP bridge that adds about 1.5s per round trip. During attach, the slowest replies take 6-8s. That is the read of the target's large register description. With a 5s timeout, lldb dropped the connection mid-attach. A 5s default fails for those users, and 15s leaves about 2x headroom over the worst observed reply.

**What decides the value.** The timeout has to cover the slowest legitimate single reply on any supported link. It is not tuned to the typical reply. The observation that local stubs answer in milliseconds is correct, but it only describes the fast case. The timeout is a ceiling on the worst case, so the median doesn't determine it. A slow reply, such as a register description, a large memory read or a bridged link, is indistinguishable from a hung stub until the timer expires. sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
Your error is the intended behavior. The sources are `mlir/docs/Tokens.md`, the LangRef section on tokens, and `BuiltinTypes.td:1265`.

## Why `AnyType` rejects tokens
`CommonTypeConstraints.td:179` defines `AnyType` as `Type<Neg<IsTokenTypePred>, "any non-token type">`. Tokens are carved out on purpose. Ops declared before tokens existed, such as `scf.if`, `scf.yield` and `arith.select`, all use `AnyType` for values they forward. Without the carve-out, any of them would silently accept a token. An op has to opt in by naming `Token` explicitly. That's why the error says "variadic of any non-token type".

## Why tokens can't be forwarded
A token is meant to be a pointer to a specific op (an `OpResult`) or a specific region (an entry block argument). From any use you should be able to walk back and say "this came from *that* op".

Forwarding breaks that guarantee. If a token goes through a yield, a branch operand or an `arith.select`, the use sees a merged value. It could come from either `%a` or `%b`, so it no longer identifies one definition.

The LangRef forbids tokens as:
- forwarded operands or results of `CallOpInterface` ops;
- argument or result types of `FunctionOpInterface` ops;
- successor operands of `BranchOpInterface` ops;
- block arguments of non-entry blocks;
- iter-args, region results or yielded values of `RegionBranchOpInterface` ops;
- results of ops that select or merge values they don't understand.

## Why tokens are SSA values
The doc gives the rationale in three points:
- **No parallel def-use system:** tokens reuse the existing SSA def-use machinery. Nothing changes in the generic op syntax, the bytecode format or the core `Operation` APIs.
- **Unidirectional like normal def-use:** a use points at its definition and not the reverse. A pass can delete a token use without touching or inspecting the definition.
- **Isolation for free:** SSA values can't cross `IsolatedFromAbove` boundaries. That lets passes process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

## Handing a token into `func.func`
This doesn't work for two reasons:
1. `func.func` is a `FunctionOpInterface` op, and token argument or result types are forbidden there.
2. `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, so no SSA value, token or otherwise, can be captured from the enclosing scope.

Both rules protect the same invariant: a token must stay tied to one definition inside one isolated region.

## What to use instead
The doc says: "When a token-like dependency must cross such a boundary, another mechanism must be used (e.g. a symbolic reference using an attribute)." In practice:
- **Symbol reference:** give the producing op or region a symbol name, and refer to it with a `SymbolRefAttr` in the callee or on the consuming op. This is the doc's suggestion.
- **Keep the consumer in the token's region:** if the consumer can live in the same region, use the token directly there. Region-bearing ops with `TokenProducerTrait` can give the body an entry-block token argument.
- **A different type:** if you need to pass or merge the value, it isn't really a token. Use a regular type, such as an index or handle type your dialect defines, so it can flow through yields, branches and calls.

For your `scf.if`, you can't return the token from either branch. Either do the consuming work inside each branch, or switch to a non-token handle type if the value has to merge.

I haven't checked how `TokenProducerTrait` or `TokenConsumerTrait` are verified, or whether other dialects use `Token`. Say if you want me to look at those.

sent.prompt: I'm reading the AArch64 Lightweight Fault Isolation (LFI) target. Three things look odd: the sandboxing rewrites are applied in the assembler rather than as a codegen pass; when an instruction loads x30, the guard that pulls it back into the sandbox is not emitted right after it but only at the next control-flow instruction; and the sandbox is fixed at 4GiB and must be 4GiB-aligned even though the code keeps full 64-bit pointers. Why each of these?

output.text:
All three come from design statements in `llvm/docs/LFI.md` and from the rewriter code. The docs only partly explain the first and third, so I've marked which parts are stated and which I inferred.

## 1. Rewrites happen in the assembler, not as a codegen pass

`LFI.md:51-53` says the rewrites are applied "at the very end of the LLVM compilation pipeline (during the assembler step). This allows the rewrites to be applied to hand-written assembly, including inline assembly."

- **Compatibility goal:** the doc's first goal (`LFI.md:14-17`) is to sandbox existing C/C++/assembly libraries unmodified. A codegen pass would never see `.s` files or inline `asm`, and those could contain any unsafe instruction.
- **Security goal:** the doc wants the compiler elements to be "simple and verifiable". A rewriter at the `MCStreamer` boundary sees exactly the instructions that end up in the object file. Nothing later can add an unchecked instruction, so you don't have to trust ISel, the scheduler, or the other backend passes.
- **Opt-out:** `.lfi_rewrite_disable` and `.lfi_rewrite_enable` (`LFI.md:79-96`) are assembler directives. This is how already-safe hand-written code is exempted.
- **Mechanism:** `MCLFIRewriter::rewriteInst` takes each `MCInst` and an `MCStreamer &Out` (`AArch64MCLFIRewriter.h:54`). It also has `onLabel` and `finish` hooks (`:57-58`).

The "simple and verifiable" reasoning is partly my inference from the stated goals. The doc doesn't spell it out as the reason for this choice.

## 2. The x30 guard is deferred to the next control-flow instruction

The reason is pointer authentication (PAC). `LFI.md:297-303` and the comment at `AArch64MCLFIRewriter.h:64-69` both give it.

- **The problem:** the guard `add x30, x27, w30, uxtw` keeps only the low 32 bits of x30. It replaces the upper bits with the sandbox base. A PAC-signed return address keeps its signature in those upper bits.
- **Example:** with `-mbranch-protection=pac-ret`, a function epilogue is `ldp ..., x30, [...]`, then `autiasp`, then `ret`. If the guard ran right after the `ldp`, it would wipe the signature, and `autiasp` would then authenticate a corrupted value.
- **Deferral:** `rewriteLRModification` emits the original instruction and sets `DeferredLRGuard = true` (`AArch64MCLFIRewriter.cpp:484-497`). The guard is flushed before a return, indirect branch, call or branch (`:922-928`). `autiasp` is not one of those, so it runs first on the intact signed pointer. The guard then lands between `autiasp` and `ret`, as the table at `LFI.md:361-370` shows.
- **Other flush points:**
  - Before a non-temporary label, because a label is a possible branch target (`:307-312`).
  - At end of stream (`:319-323`).
- **Authenticated returns:** `retaa` and `retab` expand to their own authenticate, guard and `ret` sequence. The code therefore discards any pending deferred guard first (`:914-919`). Masking before authentication would corrupt the signature.
- **Safety:** the invariant "x30 always holds a sandbox address" is briefly false between the load and the guard. No control transfer can happen in that window, so it is never observable.

The doc also notes a limit (`LFI.md:344-348`). Without `FEAT_FPAC`, a failed authentication produces a poisoned pointer, and the mask overwrites that poison. The result is still confined to the sandbox, but the authentication failure is silenced.

## 3. Fixed 4GiB sandbox, 4GiB-aligned, with full 64-bit pointers

`LFI.md:132-136` states: "The current design only supports 4GiB sandboxes, which requires the sandbox base address to be 4GiB-aligned. This is because LFI's ABI stores pointers as their full 64-bit values, rather than just 32-bit offsets from the base."

- **Why alignment is required:** every guard is `add xD, x27, wN, uxtw`. That zero-extends the low 32 bits of the pointer and adds the base `x27`. This is also the free `[x27, wM, uxtw]` addressing mode. If the base is 4GiB-aligned, the low 32 bits of a pointer already equal its offset within the sandbox. Because the pointer stored in memory is the full address, the guard only has to replace the high 32 bits with `x27`'s. Code never needs to convert between pointers and offsets.
- **Why full 64-bit pointers:** the doc gives two benefits.
  - It enables stores-only mode (`+no-lfi-loads`), where loads are not sandboxed and so must work on ordinary pointers.
  - The host can pass pointers straight into the sandbox with no translation.
- **Why it's fixed at 4GiB:** the guard is hard-wired to `uxtw`, a 32-bit extend. A different size would need a different masking scheme.
- **Compatibility:** a 32-bit offset ABI would not match existing code, which assumes ordinary 64-bit pointers. That conflicts with the "compile existing code unmodified" goal.

The doc's wording ("the current design") suggests this is a limitation of the present design and not a permanent rule. It doesn't say which other sizes were considered.

output.text:
**No. LLVM's AI Tool Use Policy (`llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`) rules out all three parts of your bot.**

## Your three pieces

1. **Picking up `good first issue` items and having an AI fix them.** This is explicitly forbidden (lines 56-62). The policy says that "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden." It applies whether or not you're a newcomer.
2. **Opening the PR autonomously.** The policy requires a human in the loop. Contributors must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone to review it. They must also be able to answer questions about it. The policy specifically bans agents that act in project spaces without human approval, and it names the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example (lines 47-49).
3. **An AI reviewer that posts comments automatically.** This is also banned. "Automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed" (lines 49-51). The policy covers comments and feedback on PRs as well as code (line 36).

## What is allowed

- Using any tool to help write a contribution, as long as a human reviews it and is accountable for it. The contributor is always the author.
- Opt-in review tools that keep a human in the loop. For example, an AI drafts review comments and a person reads, edits and posts them.
- Labelling contributions that contain substantial tool-generated content. Use a note in the PR description or a commit trailer such as `Assisted-by: <tool>`. The labelling exists to help reviewers, not to track which parts of LLVM are generated.
- Writing PR descriptions yourself. This is strongly recommended. Tools can help with translation or copy-editing.
- Contributors remain responsible for copyright and licensing of anything an AI produces.
- The one existing exception is the approved Bazel-fixer bot. Any future exception is judged individually on whether it helps the project or extracts work from maintainers (lines 148-156). You'd need to go through an RFC.

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Reviewer time is the scarce resource.** The policy calls unreviewed LLM output an "extractive contribution". It shifts the work from the author to the maintainers, who have to do the design and code review. The golden rule is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review (lines 66-95).
- **`good first issue` items are for teaching.** These issues are usually not urgent. They exist so new contributors can learn the codebase. Automating the fix wastes that, and it adds little value to the project (lines 56-62). The policy also says that passing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow" (lines 17-19).
- **Accountability needs a person.** A bot can't answer review questions or take responsibility for its work. That's why the policy requires a human in the loop for both authoring and reviewing.
- **Maintainers decide what counts as extractive.** If a PR looks non-compliant, they can paste a standard response, apply the `extractive` label, and escalate to moderators if the contributor doesn't improve it (lines 110-132). A bot like yours would likely trigger this repeatedly.

## What you could build instead

- A tool that helps a person triage issues, as long as it doesn't fix `good first issue` items.
- A review assistant that drafts comments privately, so a human reads, edits and posts them.
- If you think a bot would really benefit the project, propose it as an RFC on Discourse, as the Bazel-fixer bot did.

sent.prompt: Flang is getting a `fir.assert` operation for the checks that get lost when HLFIR and FIR passes inline runtime calls. Flang already does a few inline checks with `fir.if` plus a call to `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`, and MLIR already has `cf.assert`. Why a new op instead of either of those, why does `fir.assert` hand back 'guarded' copies of values, and what goes wrong for users today that it is meant to fix?

output.text:
`fir.assert` and its design doc (`flang/docs/InlineRuntimeChecks.md`) are already in this checkout. The op is defined at `flang/include/flang/Optimizer/Dialect/FIROps.td:84`. The answers below come from the doc, which is marked a draft design. I haven't built or run anything.

## What goes wrong for users today

Flang leaves most dynamic checks to the Fortran runtime: shape conformance, allocation status, intrinsic argument consistency. When an HLFIR or FIR pass replaces a runtime call with inline code, the check disappears with the call. That has three effects:

1. **Behavior changes with the optimization level.** The inlining passes mostly run at `-O1` and above. A non-conforming program stops with a clear message at `-O0` and does something else at `-O2`.
2. **Missing checks become memory errors.** The inlined loops take their bounds from one operand and index another. A mismatch in `DOT_PRODUCT`, `MATMUL` or array assignment becomes an out-of-bounds read or write instead of an error. A `2x3 = 3x2` assignment is a related case: the runtime only compares element counts, so it passes there and gives a wrong element order. The inline code would run out of bounds.
3. **Some checks the standard requires are missing on every path.** Inline ALLOCATE and DEALLOCATE of intrinsic-type allocatables don't check allocation status. `-mllvm -use-alloc-runtime` is the current workaround.

## Why not `fir.if` plus `_FortranAReportFatalUserError`

- **No data dependence.** Nothing ties the check to the operation it protects, so a pass can move that operation above the check. MLIR has no notion of an operation that may not return.
- **Blocks optimization.** The call has unknown memory effects, so alias-based optimizations stop at it.
- **LLVM isn't told the call never returns.** The FIR declaration has no `noreturn`, so LLVM can't use the checked condition afterwards.

## Why not `cf.assert`

- It writes the default resource, so it blocks store-to-load forwarding and load CSE across it.
- It doesn't order non-speculatable operations that have no memory effects, such as `arith.remsi`, after it.
- It lowers to `puts` plus `abort`, not the Fortran runtime's `fatal Fortran runtime error(file:line): ...` format.
- It has no guarded results.

The doc also rejects the result-less `fir.assert` from PR #223287, which converts to `cf.assert` and patches LICM. That fix protects one pass. Every other pass that moves or recreates operations would need the same fix. If a protected load or remainder ends up above the check, LLVM can infer from its undefined behavior that the check can't fail, and delete it.

## Why it returns guarded copies

The op is written `%g = fir.assert %ok, kind, "msg" values(...) guard(%x)`. When the condition holds, each result equals the matching guarded operand. Otherwise the program terminates through the runtime.

Operations that must not run before the check consume `%g` instead of `%x`. The ordering is then enforced by SSA dominance, so no pass has to know about `fir.assert`. Moving the protected operation above the check is impossible, because its operand doesn't exist until the check has run.

Two consequences follow from this:

- **Rewrites can't look through the op.** The op isn't a view and isn't speculatable. A fold that replaced `%g` with `%x` would silently drop the dependence. Analyses such as alias analysis and origin finding are allowed to look through it.
- **What gets guarded.** For conformance checks you guard the arrays being accessed, not the extents. That keeps constant loop bounds visible to loop optimizations.

The effect model, `MemWrite<FortranRuntimeResource>`, uses a non-addressable resource. DCE keeps the assert, and it stays ordered with calls and I/O. It doesn't touch user memory, so load CSE and forwarding keep working. Code generation lowers it to a `cond_br` to a `noreturn` runtime call, so LLVM gets the information too.

The doc also considers a region-based assert like `shape.assuming`. It rejects that because the region boundary gets in the way of the single-block patterns the checks must not block, such as `OptimizedBufferization` and store-to-load forwarding.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start contributing to ClangIR. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
# ClangIR (CIR) for a newcomer

**What it is.** CIR is a high-level IR for C/C++ built as an MLIR dialect. It sits between Clang's AST and LLVM IR, and it keeps language-level structure that LLVM IR loses. It lives inside the Clang project and is not a standalone in-tree dialect.

**Pipeline and how to enable it.** The path is AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM IR → backend.
- Pass `-fclangir` to the driver to compile through CIR.
- Pass `-emit-cir` to see the CIR. It is the CIR counterpart of `-emit-llvm`.
- Building Clang with `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` removes CIR and makes `-fclangir` unavailable.

**Why codegen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught.**
- CIRGen deliberately mirrors classic CodeGen: the same structure, similar names, and often duplicated logic. This was judged the surest way to get equivalent output, and it lets you compare the two side by side to find what is missing or wrong.
- The cost is real technical debt. Fixes and features in classic codegen have to be ported by hand. For now the project accepts this duplication. Refactoring to share code is left to the developer's and reviewers' judgement, and larger sharing waits for a long-term plan.
- Divergence is caught mainly by the lit tests. Each CIR codegen test carries two sets of LLVM IR checks. One covers the CIR→LLVM path and the other covers classic codegen's output.
  - When you write the test, you compare the two by hand. Any difference should be a known missing feature, or you fix it in the same PR.
  - Afterwards the classic-codegen checks act as sentinels. If classic behaviour changes, the test fails, and the ClangIR contributors are expected to update CIR.
- Planned later: automatic equivalence checks (for example `opt -pass-normalize` or Alive2), and running the whole classic codegen test suite through the CIR path.

**Cleanups and exceptions.**
- CIRGen follows classic codegen's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop model to drive the cleanup scopes. The CIR it produces is structured, not unstructured like classic LLVM IR.
- High-level form:
  - `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup [normal|eh|all] { … }` represents a scope that needs cleanup.
  - Nesting scopes gives destructors in reverse construction order.
  - `cir.break`, `cir.continue`, `cir.return` and `cir.goto` implicitly run the cleanup region on the way out.
  - `cir.try` has catch regions and an unwind region. They receive a `!cir.eh_token`, and `cir.begin_catch` / `cir.end_catch` bracket each handler.
- Lowering happens in three stages:
  1. **Flattening.** The flatten-CFG pass (`cir::FlattenCFG`; the design doc also calls it `cir::LowerCFG`) turns regions into explicit blocks. It reuses classic codegen's slot-and-dispatch scheme for branching through cleanups. Throwing calls become `cir.try_call` with an unwind destination that starts with `cir.eh.initiate`. Dispatch uses `cir.eh.dispatch`, and `cir.begin_cleanup` / `cir.end_cleanup` bracket EH cleanups. A throwing call inside an EH cleanup ends in `cir.eh.terminate`. This form is still ABI-agnostic.
  2. **EH ABI lowering.** A separate, planned pass runs after flattening and before CIR→LLVM. It adds the personality function and target-specific operations.
     - For Itanium, `cir.eh.landingpad` plus compare-and-branch on type ids replaces initiate/dispatch, and `__cxa_begin_catch` / `__cxa_end_catch` calls replace begin/end catch.
     - For the Microsoft ABI, it uses `catchswitch`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad` and the matching return operations.
  3. **Lowering to the LLVM dialect.**
- This pass is described as "will be introduced", and the doc is a design, so check what has landed in the code before relying on it.

**Calling-convention lowering.**
- Classification lives in the shared LLVM ABI library (`llvm/lib/ABI/`). That library is the single source of truth: `abi::Type*`, `ABIInfo`, and the X86_64 and AArch64 targets.
- An MLIR adapter layer sits on top of it:
  - `ABITypeMapper` maps `mlir::Type` to `abi::Type*`. CIR may need dialect-aware mapping because `cir::IntType` is not `mlir::IntegerType`.
  - An ABI lowering pass runs these steps:
    1. Read the signature through `FunctionOpInterface`.
    2. Map the types.
    3. Call `ABIInfo::computeInfo`.
    4. Rewrite the function and its call sites, including expand, indirect/sret, and coerce.
- Each dialect (CIR, FIR) implements only `ABIRewriteContext`, which creates the operations (`createFunction`, `createCall`, `createExtractValue`, …).
- A target registry picks the `ABIInfo` from the triple.
- The goal is call-compatibility with classic Clang CodeGen, validated by differential testing. Variadics are handled on x86_64 only, for now.

**Where it is written down** (all under `clang/docs/CIR/`):

| Topic | File |
|---|---|
| Overview, usage, RFCs, talks, history | `index.md` |
| Duplication strategy and testing | `CodeDuplication.md` |
| Cleanup and EH design (large, with many CIR examples) | `CleanupAndEHDesign.md` |
| Calling-convention lowering | `ABILowering.md` |

I read these docs through the notes and did not read the source under `clang/lib/CIR/`. The docs contain design intent ("will be introduced", "being proposed"), so check which parts are implemented before you build on them. The best places to start are the `ClangIR`-labelled issues and PRs on llvm-project, and the existing codegen tests that have both CIR and classic LLVM check lines.

sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
Your tree documents this in `mlir/docs/Tokens.md`. The rest is what that doc says.

**Why `AnyType` rejects tokens**

A token is meant to be a pointer to a specific op, reached through an OpResult, or to a region, reached through an entry block argument. The point is that from any use you can walk back to "this token came from *that* op". That only holds if nothing merges or forwards tokens. `scf.yield`, `scf.if` results, `cf.br` operands and `arith.select` all have forwarding semantics, so they would make the origin ambiguous. At `%t = scf.if ... -> token` you could no longer say which branch's producer `%t` came from.

To prevent this, tokens are excluded from the default `AnyType` constraint in ODS (`CommonTypeConstraints.td`). `scf.if` results and `scf.yield` operands are `Variadic<AnyType>`, so the verifier says "must be variadic of any non-token type". An op only accepts tokens if it opts in with the `Token` constraint. ODS then adds `TokenProducerTrait` or `TokenConsumerTrait` automatically.

**Where tokens can't flow**

The LangRef contract forbids tokens in these places:
- forwarded operands or results of `CallOpInterface` ops
- argument or result types of `FunctionOpInterface` ops
- successor operands of `BranchOpInterface` ops
- block arguments of non-entry blocks
- iter-args, region results or yielded values of `RegionBranchOpInterface` ops
- results of ops that select or merge values they don't understand, such as `arith.select`

**Why SSA values**

SSA lets one op refer to another without a second, parallel def-use system for operations. It reuses the existing use-list machinery and needs no changes to the generic op syntax, the bytecode format or the core `Operation` APIs. The chain is also one-directional: a use points at its definition. A transformation can drop a token use without inspecting or touching the producer.

**Why `func.func` doesn't work**

There are two reasons:
1. A function's argument and result types are a `FunctionOpInterface` position, and tokens are forbidden there.
2. `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, and tokens are ordinary SSA values, so they can't cross that boundary. This is deliberate. It lets passes process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

**What to use instead**

The doc says that when a token-like dependency must cross an isolated boundary, you need another mechanism, such as a symbolic reference using an attribute. In practice:
- Give the target op a symbol or name, and have the function refer to it with a `SymbolRefAttr` or a similar attribute.
- If the callee needs a runtime handle, pass a regular type, such as an integer, an opaque pointer or a dialect-specific handle type. Tokens carry no runtime data, so this is a different concept.
- If you only need the token inside the body, create it there. An op in the body can produce it, or the body's own region can provide it as an entry block argument if the parent op has `TokenProducerTrait`.

For your `scf.if`, you have to restructure so the token isn't merged across branches. For example, produce the token once outside the `if` and use it from inside, or put the token-consuming op inside each branch.

sent.prompt: I'd like to automate some of our contribution work: a bot that picks up issues labelled `good first issue`, has an AI coding agent write the fix and open the pull request by itself, and an AI reviewer that posts its comments on incoming PRs automatically. Would the project accept that? What does it require of contributions made with AI tools, and why does it draw the lines where it does?

output.text:
**No, the project would not accept that bot.** All three parts conflict with `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## What the policy says about your three parts

**1. A bot that fixes `good first issue` issues with an AI agent.** This is explicitly forbidden. The policy says: "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden." It says this applies "whether you are a newcomer or not". It also makes no exception for human review of the output.

**2. An agent that opens PRs by itself.** The policy "bans agents that take action in our digital spaces without human approval", and gives the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example. LLVM's core rule is a **human in the loop**. The contributor must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone else to review it. The contributor is always the author and must be able to answer questions about the work. An autonomous bot has no human author who can do that.

**3. An AI reviewer that posts comments automatically.** This is also banned: "automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed." Comments and feedback on PRs are listed as covered contributions.

## What is allowed

- Use whatever tools you like to write your own contributions, as long as you review and understand them and can defend them in review.
- An opt-in review tool that keeps a human in the loop is acceptable. For example, a tool drafts comments and a person reads, edits and chooses to post them.
- Using an LLM to draft documentation, then checking it for correctness, editing it and posting it yourself, is called an approved use.
- Label contributions with substantial tool-generated content, in the PR description, the commit message, or a trailer such as `Assisted-by: <tool>`.
- Write PR descriptions yourself (tools for translation or copy-editing are fine). They should cover motivation, approach, impact and open questions.
- You are responsible for copyright. Regenerating copyrighted material with an AI tool doesn't remove the copyright.
- There is one existing exception, the Bazel-fixer bot. The project council approved it through an RFC. Any future exception is judged individually on whether it helps the project or extracts work from maintainers, so an RFC on Discourse would be the route.

## Why the lines are drawn there

- **Extractive contributions.** Reviewing takes scarce maintainer time. Sending unreviewed LLM output pushes the design and code review work onto maintainers. The "golden rule" is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review. An automated pipeline can produce PRs and comments much faster than humans can review them.
- **`good first issue` exists for people.** These issues are usually not urgent. Their purpose is to let newcomers learn the codebase and grow into long-term contributors. Automating them removes that learning opportunity and adds little value. The policy also says that passing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow."
- **Accountability.** A bot can't answer review questions or take responsibility for its changes, and a named human can.
- **Enforcement.** Maintainers can reply with a standard "doesn't comply" message and apply the `extractive` label. Repeat violations get escalated to the moderation or admin team, who can lock the conversation.

## What you could do instead

- Build a local assistant that helps individual contributors investigate bugs, draft patches or draft review comments. A person must review everything and decide what to post.
- Point it at issues that are not labelled `good first issue`.
- Offer it as an opt-in tool for humans, not an account that posts on its own.
- If you want something fully automated, propose it as an RFC on Discourse, as the Bazel-fixer bot did. Treat it as unlikely to be approved unless it clearly saves maintainers work, for example by producing machine-checkable proofs like the Alive2 example the policy cites.

**Recommendation: don't revert to 5s as the default.** Keep 15s, and give people who want fast hang detection a per-session override.

**What decides the value.** The timeout has to cover the slowest legitimate reply, not the typical one. Local stubs answer in milliseconds, but the default applies to every gdb-remote user. Commit 4a5bdd555 gives the reason it was raised. Velmora boards sit behind a serial-over-IP bridge that adds about 1.5s per round trip. During attach, the slowest reply (reading the large target register description) takes 6-8s. With 5s, lldb dropped the connection mid-attach, so the 5s default was a functional bug for those users. The comment next to the value in `ProcessGDBRemoteProperties.td:9-12` records this.

**Why a revert isn't safe.**
- Velmora attach would break again, because 6-8s replies exceed 5s.
- The local-stub case is a poor argument. A fast stub is not hurt by a higher timeout, because the timeout only matters when no reply arrives. The only cost of 15s is that a truly hung stub takes 15s to notice instead of 5s.
- The sanitized-build default is already 60s, so the project already accepts slower hang detection when the environment needs it.

**Better options for the person who wants fast failure.**
- Set it in `~/.lldbinit`: `settings set plugin.process.gdb-remote.packet-timeout 5`. It is a Global setting, so this works with no code change.
- If local-vs-remote tuning matters across many users, a larger change could pick the timeout by connection type. For example, a lower value for `localhost` or unix-socket connections. I haven't checked how the plugin would support that.

**If you still want to lower the default:** the lowest safe value is just above the slowest known legitimate reply plus margin. For Velmora that is roughly 10s or more, not 5s. I haven't measured anything. Those numbers come from the commit message.

Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
The behaviour you hit is deliberate, and it's described in `mlir/docs/Tokens.md` and `mlir/include/mlir/IR/CommonTypeConstraints.td:176-183`.

## Why `AnyType` rejects tokens

`AnyType` is defined as `Type<Neg<IsTokenTypePred>, "any non-token type">`. It used to mean "anything". Now it means "anything except `TokenType`". A token is a pointer to one specific op (through its `OpResult`) or to one specific region (through an entry block argument). Many ops accept `AnyType` and move values around without understanding them, such as `scf.if`, `scf.yield` and `arith.select`. Excluding tokens from `AnyType` means an op has to opt in to tokens by declaring `Token` explicitly. It can't take one by accident.

## Why tokens can't be forwarded

The purpose of a token is that from any use you can walk back and say "this came from that specific op". Forwarding breaks that. After `scf.if` merges two `my.token.produce` results, or `arith.select` picks one, or a `cf.br` passes one into a block argument, the value could come from either producer, depending on runtime control flow. The doc lists the forbidden positions:

- forwarded operands or results of `CallOpInterface` ops
- argument or result types of `FunctionOpInterface` ops
- successor operands of `BranchOpInterface` ops
- block arguments of non-entry blocks
- iter-args, region results and yielded values of `RegionBranchOpInterface` ops
- results of any op that selects or merges values it doesn't understand

Your `scf.if` fails twice: its result is `Variadic<AnyType>`, and so are the `scf.yield` operands.

## Why tokens are SSA values

The design rationale in the doc is that SSA already provides def-use machinery, so tokens need no parallel system for one op to refer to another. There are no changes to the generic op syntax, the bytecode format or the core `Operation` APIs. Def-use chains are also one-directional: the use points at the definition. A transform can delete a token use without looking at or touching the producer.

## Why a token can't go into a `func.func` body

There are two separate reasons:

1. **Function signatures can't carry tokens.** A `FunctionOpInterface` op can't have a token as an argument or result type. Calls are forwarding positions too, so the caller's operand and the callee's block argument would be a forwarded token.
2. **Isolation.** `func.func` is `IsolatedFromAbove`, so a token can't be captured from outside either. The doc says this is intentional, so passes can process isolated regions concurrently without racing on def-use chains.

## What to use instead

The doc says: "When a token-like dependency must cross such a boundary, another mechanism must be used (e.g. a symbolic reference using an attribute)." In practice:

- Name the thing with a `SymbolRefAttr` or `StringAttr`/`IntegerAttr` ID. The producer carries the symbol or ID, and the consumer inside the function looks it up by that name, as `func.call` does with the callee symbol.
- If the dependency is only ordering or "which scope am I in", put the token-consuming op and its producer in the same isolated region. Alternatively, have the region's parent op provide an entry block argument of token type. That needs `TokenProducerTrait` on the parent op, and only entry block arguments are allowed.
- If you need a runtime handle, use a different, non-token type, such as `!async.token`, `!gpu.async.token` or a plain integer or handle type. That type is an ordinary value type, so it can pass through function signatures and yields.

The `scf.if` case works the same way. If you need to pick between two producers, make the choice at the symbolic or attribute level, or restructure so the consumer lives inside each branch.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start contributing to ClangIR. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
**What CIR is, and where it sits.** ClangIR (CIR) is a high-level MLIR dialect that lives inside Clang, not as a standalone in-tree dialect. It keeps C/C++ constructs such as structured loops and scopes, and sits between the AST and LLVM IR. To use it:
- `-fclangir` compiles through CIR: AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM IR → backend.
- `-emit-cir` is the CIR equivalent of `-emit-llvm`.
- `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` at build time removes CIR from Clang, which also makes `-fclangir` unavailable.

**Why CIRGen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught.** CIRGen deliberately mirrors classic codegen's structure, names and logic. The aim is that CIR eventually lowers to LLVM IR semantically equivalent to what classic codegen produces. The near-identical code also lets you diff the two to find what's missing or wrong.

The docs call this duplication technical debt. It is accepted for now because progress matters more, and a long-term sharing strategy is still to be decided. Don't do sharing refactors unless they make sense on their own. A comment marking the opportunity is enough.

Divergence is caught by the LIT tests. Each CIR codegen test carries two sets of LLVM IR checks:
- One set checks the IR from CIR lowered to LLVM.
- The other checks the IR from classic codegen.

You compare the two when you write the test, and fix real differences in the same PR. If classic codegen changes later, these tests fail, and keeping CIR in sync is currently the ClangIR contributors' job. The stated future goal is automated equivalence checking, for example with `opt -pass-normalize` and Alive2.

**Cleanups and exceptions.** CIRGen still uses classic codegen's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/`popCleanup`, but the output is structured instead of unstructured. It has three forms.

*High-level (structured):*
- `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup normal|eh|all { … }` holds a scope's cleanup.
- Nested scopes give destructors in reverse order.
- `cir.break`, `cir.continue`, `cir.return` and `cir.goto` implicitly run the cleanup region on the way out.
- `cir.try { } catch [...] (%eh_token) { } unwind { }` represents try/catch.
- A catch handler starts with `cir.begin_catch`, and its `cir.end_catch` sits in a `cir.cleanup.scope` cleanup region.

*Flattened (`cir::FlattenCFG`, still ABI-agnostic):*
- There are no nested regions.
- Branching through cleanups uses the same destination-slot-and-switch scheme as classic codegen.
- A throwing `cir.call` becomes `cir.try_call` with normal and unwind destinations.
- The unwind block starts with `cir.eh.initiate`, which yields a `!cir.eh_token`.
- Other EH ops are `cir.eh.dispatch`, `cir.begin_cleanup`/`end_cleanup`, `cir.resume`, and `cir.eh.terminate` for a throw during EH cleanup.

*ABI-specific EH lowering* is the last stage and maps onto each target's LLVM IR EH form. The doc has a section on it, and I didn't read that section.

**Calling-convention lowering.** It is a separate pass, not part of CIRGen, with three layers:
1. `llvm/lib/ABI/` holds the shared classification (`abi::Type*`, `ABIInfo`, X86_64 and AArch64 targets). This is the single source of truth for ABI rules, and it's meant to be reusable by FIR.
2. An MLIR adapter maps `mlir::Type` to `abi::Type*` (`ABITypeMapper`) and drives the rewriting.
3. Each dialect implements only `ABIRewriteContext` (`CIRABIRewriteContext` for CIR). It has `rewriteFunctionDefinition` and `rewriteCallSite`, and it sets attributes like sret and byval.

For CIR, the pass pipeline order is:
1. `cir-target-lowering`
2. `cir-cxxabi-lowering`
3. `cir-call-conv-lowering`

The last pass needs a `dlti.dl_spec` attribute on the module. It is on by default only for x86_64, since that is the only classifier implemented so far. `-fno-clangir-call-conv-lowering` and `-fclangir-call-conv-lowering` are `-cc1` options, so pass them through `-Xclang`. Classifier code is under `clang/lib/CIR/Dialect/Transforms/`.

**Where each part is written down** (all in `clang/docs/CIR/`):
- `index.md` covers the overview, usage, RFCs, talks and history.
- `CodeDuplication.md` covers the mirroring rationale, the dual-check testing strategy and the long-term plan.
- `CleanupAndEHDesign.md` covers cleanups and EH, with many CIR examples. It also has a section on dynamic exception specifications.
- `ABILowering.md` covers calling-convention lowering, including its open questions.

I only read the notes and docs, not the implementation. Check pass names and flags against the code before relying on them, because the docs describe a design that is still changing.

sent.prompt: In MLIR I have an op that produces a value of the builtin `token` type, and I tried to return it from both branches of an `scf.if`; the verifier says the result 'must be variadic of any non-token type'. Why doesn't `AnyType` accept tokens, and why can't a token flow through yields, branches or selects like any other SSA value? Why are tokens SSA values at all rather than some other way for one op to point at another? And I want to hand a token into a `func.func` body: why won't that work, and what should I use instead?

output.text:
**Why `AnyType` rejects tokens.** In `CommonTypeConstraints.td`, `AnyType` now means "any non-token type", which is what it meant before tokens existed. A token is a pointer to a specific op (through an OpResult) or to a region (through an entry block argument). The rule is that you can always walk back from a use and say "this token came from *that* op". Ops that forward values, like `scf.if`, `scf.yield` and `cf.br`, declare their operands and results as `AnyType`. If `AnyType` accepted tokens, any such op could accidentally merge or relay them. Excluding tokens by default makes forwarding opt-in. An op that wants a token must say `Token` explicitly. This is the source of your message: `scf.if` has `Variadic<AnyType>` results and `scf.yield` has `AnyType` operands, so both reject it.

**Why tokens can't flow through yields, branches or selects.** Once a token passes through one of these, the chain is obscured. After `%t = scf.if ... yield %a / yield %b`, or an `arith.select`, `%t` no longer points to one definite op. The LangRef therefore forbids a token as:
- a forwarded operand or result of a `CallOpInterface` op;
- an argument or result type of a `FunctionOpInterface` op;
- a successor operand of a `BranchOpInterface` op;
- a block argument of a non-entry block;
- a forwarded value into or out of a `RegionBranchOpInterface` op (iter-args, region results, yields);
- the result of any op that selects or merges values it doesn't understand, such as `arith.select`.

For your case, you can't produce one token that is "either `%a` or `%b`". Pick one definite producer before the `scf.if`, or give each consumer its own token from the branch it is in.

**Why tokens are SSA values.** The design rationale is that they let one op refer to another without a new parallel def-use system. They reuse the existing SSA machinery, so the generic op syntax, the bytecode infrastructure and the core C++ APIs around `Operation` don't change. The def-use chain is also unidirectional: the use points at the definition. A transformation can remove a token use without touching or inspecting the producer.

**Why a token can't go into a `func.func` body.** There are two reasons:
- `FunctionOpInterface` ops can't have token arguments or results, as listed above.
- Because tokens are SSA values, they can't cross `IsolatedFromAbove` region boundaries. This is deliberate. It lets passes process isolated regions concurrently without racing on shared def-use chains.

**What to use instead.** The docs say that when a token-like dependency has to cross such a boundary, you need a different mechanism, for example a symbolic reference through an attribute. In practice:
- Refer to the producer by symbol, such as a `SymbolRefAttr` to a named op or global, and not by SSA value.
- Or restructure so the token's producer and consumers sit in the same isolated region. For example, put the producing op inside the function body.
- Or, if you need a value that does flow through calls and yields, define a separate non-token type or an index/ID value for that purpose.

If you want a token as an entry block argument of your own region op, the parent op must declare `TokenProducerTrait`. ODS adds that automatically for `Token`-typed results, and `TokenConsumerTrait` for `Token`-typed operands. Non-entry block token arguments are rejected.

All of this comes from `mlir/docs/Tokens.md`. I haven't read the verifier code or the LangRef section itself.

**No. The project would reject all three parts of the bot as you've described them.** The policy is in `llvm/docs/AIToolPolicy.md`.

## How each part fares

**1. Fixing `good first issue` issues with an AI agent: forbidden.**
- The policy says (lines 56–62) that "Using AI tools to fix issues labelled as 'good first issues' is forbidden." This applies to everyone, newcomer or not.
- The reason given is that these issues aren't urgent. They exist as learning opportunities for new contributors. Fully automating the fix wastes that and "doesn't add much value to the project."
- `Contributing.md` also points newcomers to these issues as a way to learn the codebase.

**2. An agent that opens PRs by itself: not allowed.**
- The core rule is a **human in the loop**. The contributor must read and review all LLM-generated code or text before asking anyone to review it. They stay the author, are fully accountable, and must be able to answer questions during review.
- Lines 47–51 say this "bans agents that take action in our digital spaces without human approval," and give the GitHub `@claude` agent as an example. An autonomous bot that opens PRs falls under that ban.

**3. An AI reviewer that posts comments automatically: not allowed.**
- The same passage says "automated review tools that publish comments without human review are not allowed."
- The policy also covers "comments and feedback on pull requests," not only code.
- An opt-in review tool that keeps a human in the loop is acceptable.

## Why the lines are drawn there

The policy's argument is about **extractive contributions**. Reviewing costs maintainer time. Sending unreviewed LLM output shifts the effort from the implementer to the reviewer. The "golden rule" is that a contribution must be worth more to the project than the time it takes to review. A bot that produces PRs at scale breaks this rule, because it generates review work without anyone vouching for it. The project also wants to grow new contributors, and the policy says that passing maintainer feedback to an LLM "doesn't help anyone grow."

## What would be accepted

- **Use AI tools yourself, with review.** You can use any tool to draft a fix, as long as you read and understand it and can defend it. The exception is `good first issue` issues.
- **Disclose substantial tool use.** Put it in the PR description or a commit trailer, for example `Assisted-by: <tool>`. The policy also strongly recommends writing the PR description yourself.
- **Keep reviews human-approved.** A review assistant is fine if you read its output and choose what to post.
- **Make PRs small and verifiable.** The policy's examples are a PR backed by an Alive2 proof and LLM-generated docs that a human checked before posting.
- **Don't post unreviewed AI content anywhere.** That includes issues, security reports, RFCs and PR comments.
- **Check copyright.** You are responsible for making sure the contribution doesn't reproduce copyrighted material.

The only existing exception is the Bazel-fixer bot, which the project council approved through an RFC. The policy says any further exception "will be considered individually on its own merits." sent.prompt: I'm about to start contributing to ClangIR. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what CIR is, where it sits in Clang's pipeline and how I turn it on; why its code generation copies classic codegen so closely and how divergence from classic codegen is caught; how C++ cleanups and exceptions are represented and lowered; how calling-convention lowering is organised; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
# ClangIR (CIR) for a newcomer

**What it is.** CIR is an MLIR dialect that lives inside Clang. It is a high-level IR that keeps C/C++ structure (scopes, loops, `cir.cleanup.scope`, `cir.try`) and sits between the AST and LLVM IR.

**Pipeline.** The path is AST → CIR → CIR passes → LLVM IR → backend. The CIR passes include `cir-target-lowering`, `cir-cxxabi-lowering`, CFG flattening and `cir-call-conv-lowering`.

**Turning it on.**
- `-fclangir` compiles through CIR.
- `-emit-cir` is the CIR counterpart of `-emit-llvm`.
- The build flag `-DCLANG_ENABLE_CIR=OFF` removes CIR, and then `-fclangir` is unavailable.

**Why codegen copies classic codegen, and how divergence is caught.**
- CIRGen deliberately mirrors `clang/lib/CodeGen`: same structure, similar names (`CIRGenModule`/`CIRGenFunction`) and often duplicated logic. That was judged the surest way to get equivalent output.
- The cost is duplication that has to be kept in sync by hand. The accepted plan is to tolerate it now and share code only once the long-term design is clear. Over time CIR is meant to get higher-level, with ABI details moved into later passes.
- Divergence is caught by LIT tests that carry two sets of LLVM IR checks. One set is for CIR lowered to LLVM IR, and the other is for classic codegen's direct output.
- You compare the two sets when you write a test and fix any differences that aren't known missing features.
- Those tests also act as sentinels. If someone changes classic codegen and a CIR test fails, updating CIR is the CIR contributors' job.
- `clang/include/clang/CIR/MissingFeatures.h` is in the tree. I didn't open it, so check there for how unimplemented features are tracked.

**Cleanups and exceptions.**
- Codegen still uses classic's `EHScopeStack` and `pushCleanup`/pop, but emits structured MLIR ops.
- `cir.cleanup.scope { body } cleanup [normal|eh|all] { ... }` models cleanups. `break`, `continue`, `return` and `goto` that leave the scope implicitly run the cleanup first.
- `cir.try` has catch regions and an unwind region. Handlers receive a `!cir.eh_token` and use `cir.begin_catch`/`cir.end_catch`.
- Partial array cleanup is a cleanup region on `cir.array.ctor`, expanded in `LoweringPrepare`.
- Lowering happens in stages:
  1. The flattening pass (documented as `cir::FlattenCFG`/`LowerCFG`) makes control flow block-based and still ABI-agnostic. It uses a cleanup destination slot plus `cir.switch.flat`, as classic does. Throwing calls become `cir.try_call`, and the EH ops are `cir.eh.initiate`, `eh.dispatch`, `begin_cleanup`/`end_cleanup` and `eh.terminate`.
  2. An EH ABI-lowering pass then turns those into Itanium form: `cir.eh.landingpad`, `__cxa_begin_catch`/`__cxa_end_catch`, `__clang_call_terminate`, and a personality function.
- I only read the first ~1,250 of 2,050 lines of that doc. The remaining part is probably more Itanium examples, but I haven't confirmed that.

**Calling-convention lowering.**
- Classification is not done in CIR. It lives in the shared LLVM ABI library at `llvm/lib/ABI/`, which works on its own `abi::Type*`.
- On the MLIR side, `ABITypeMapper` converts `mlir::Type` to `abi::Type*`. A generic ABI pass calls the library's `ABIInfo`, then rewrites signatures and call sites through a per-dialect `ABIRewriteContext`. CIR's is `CIRABIRewriteContext`, and FIR can reuse the rest.
- The CIR pass `cir-call-conv-lowering` runs after `cir-target-lowering` and `cir-cxxabi-lowering`. It needs a `dlti.dl_spec` attribute on the module.
- It runs by default only on x86_64, which is the only classifier implemented so far. `-fclangir-call-conv-lowering` and `-fno-clangir-call-conv-lowering` are `-cc1` flags, so use `-Xclang` from the driver.
- The doc itself says the library is partly unmerged and AArch64 isn't implemented, so check the actual code before relying on any of this.

**Where it's written down.**

| Topic | Where |
|---|---|
| Overview, usage, RFCs, talks | `clang/docs/CIR/index.md` |
| Duplication strategy and testing | `clang/docs/CIR/CodeDuplication.md` |
| Cleanups and EH | `clang/docs/CIR/CleanupAndEHDesign.md` |
| Calling-convention lowering | `clang/docs/CIR/ABILowering.md` |
| Code | `clang/lib/CIR/` (`CodeGen`, `Lowering`, `Dialect`) |
| Op, type and attribute definitions | `clang/include/clang/CIR/Dialect/IR/*.td` |

Upstream discussion is under the `ClangIR` label on llvm-project issues and PRs.
